catalog_quote: [Sandy 2017:42] Tone and stress have an impoverished distribution in Karuk. Each accented word bears exactly one stress and at most one H tone, and follows the pattern of a span of H tone followed by a span of L tone ... Words that are lexically unaccented surface with a final H tone, unless at the right edge of an utterance, in which case they are toneless. Stress coincides with the syllable containing the H-tone-bearing mora (at the right edge of the H span), when present, thus marking the surface contrastive tone in the word. In the absence of a surface H tone, stress falls on a long vowel when present, otherwise, stress is final. While any syllable, from the first to the final, can bear prominence, striking patterns, alternations and gaps make it seem that generalizations regarding the placement of prominence in a stem should be possible. ... sweep_summary: Only one bibliography title matched the stress/accent/prosody search for Karuk: Sandy 2017, Prosodic Prominence in Karuk (UC Berkeley dissertation, eScholarship 6pg1s3h3), which is already the catalog's deciding source and was already held by the project (the weight-sensitive languages 2026-09-12). I re-read the deciding passages in the text layer (sec. 2.5.1 pp.42-43, sec. 2.5.2 p.45, sec. 5.1.1 p.93) and they are verbatim as quoted in the catalog: one stress per accented word, on the syllable bearing the privative H tone; default long-vowel-else-final only in lexically unaccented words (final H attributed to an AP boundary tone); high-before-long else penult in derived words; stress predictable from tone but not vice versa. The catalog's classification 'tonal' is confirmed. Beyond the listed item I read Bright 1957 first-hand (open PDF from linguistics.berkeley.edu/~karuk, previously held under our earlier reading): p.13 allophone c) matches the StressTyp2-carried passage 1153 word for word (with the examples StressTyp2 omitted), p.12 defines accented syllables as strong stress plus high/falling pitch, and p.49 sec. 383 states the recessive (pre-last-long-vowel, else penult) accentuation that Sandy calls high-before-long, so the carried primary is now verified and the catalog can cite Bright directly. Sandy's 2013 accent handouts and the 2014 WSCLA paper also confirm. Not reached: Sandy 2023 OUP chapter on Harrington's diacritics (paywalled; from its title about recovering prosodic notation, low priority), Garrett et al. 2023 De Gruyter sketch (paywalled, 405 to the fetcher; low), and Macaulay 1990 'Accent in Karok' (no open copy found; medium priority as the original privative-H analysis Sandy builds on). Files copied/downloaded into (, ) with and updated. Nothing supersedes the catalog's deciding source; Bright 1957 p.13 now carries first-hand status.

new_statements.reading: Bright's primary description, now read first-hand from the open Berkeley-hosted scan rather than carried through StressTyp2: the acute and circumflex accents are strong stress plus high-level or falling pitch, at most one per phonological word; strong stress in unaccented words is a juncture-and-pause (phrase-edge) effect falling on a long-voweled syllable if present, else the final syllable; recessive accentuation in prefixation/compounding lands on the syllable before the last long vowel, else the penult. This is exactly the system Sandy 2017 formalizes (privative H tone, stress on the H-bearing syllable, default long-vowel-else-final only in lexically unaccented words, high-before-long in derived words), so the catalog's 'tonal' coding with a weight-conditioned default stands.

audit.reasoning: The classification (tonal / pitch accent, stress parasitic on H tone, weight-sensitive default only in surface-H-less words, word domain) rests on Sandy 2017, a 235-pp Berkeley dissertation wholly on Karuk prosodic prominence, with Bright 1957 (the xi+457-pp reference grammar) carried as primary; both are held and the deciding quotations were confirmed verbatim at the stated pages (Sandy pp.42-43, 93, 195; Bright p.13 sec. 163c). Glottolog lists no larger or later prosody source; the only later items are a 2023 handbook sketch co-authored by Sandy and a 2023 OUP chapter by Sandy, both paywalled and derivative of the dissertation. Sandy 2014 (WSCLA 17) was downloaded now and independently confirms 'one stress per word.. coincides with the syllable containing the tone-bearing mora'. The StressTyp2 contradiction note (leftmost-heavy-else-final) is correctly diagnosed in the record as Bright'

sources.note: One stress per word, located on the syllable carrying the (privative, lexically or morphologically assigned) H tone; stress is parasitic on tone, and only lexically unaccented words get a default (long vowel if present, else final; p.45 attributes that final H to an Accentual-Phrase boundary H%). In derived words the unmarked 'high-before-long' pattern puts prominence on the syllable before the rightmost long vowel, else on the penult. Any syllable from first to last can bear prominence.

sources.note: First-hand confirmation of the StressTyp2-carried passage (verbatim, with 'long-voweled' hyphenated and the examples StressTyp2 dropped). Accent = strong stress + pitch (acute: high level; circumflex: falling); at most one accented syllable per phonological word; strong stress in unaccented words is a prepausal effect (juncture.. pause), on a long-voweled syllable if present else final; recessive accentuation in prefixation/compounding puts the acute on the syllable before the last long vowel, else penult (antepenult for..VCa).

sources.quote: Each Karuk word has at most one accent. The syllable with the written accent is always stressed. A vowel written with acute accent has level high pitch ... A vowel written with circumflex accent has pitch that falls from high to low ... Depending on what the accent is, and where it is in the word, the pitches (or tune) of the rest of the word are all predictable
sources.note: Pedagogical restatement of Bright: one accent per word, stress on the accented syllable; pitch contours predictable from the accent position.
